title: Bullpen
tagline: Bullpen turns AI agents into employees: describe your business, Gemini hires the team, routes every task automatically, and gets smarter from your feedback.
description: Inspiration Most AI products are built around one chatbot. We wanted to explore a different idea: what if using AI felt more like managing a team? Bullpen was inspired by how real teams divide work between specialists. A researcher gathers information, a writer creates content, and a designer turns that content into visuals. Instead of relying on one AI model to do everything, Bullpen allows users to create specialized AI agents and assign tasks based on their strengths. The name Bullpen represents a group of specialists who are ready to step in whenever their skills are needed. What it does Bullpen is a platform for creating and managing a personalized AI workforce. Users can: Describe their business and automatically generate a suggested AI team. Create agents with unique names, roles, specialties, instructions, tones, and context. Choose a Gemini model for each agent. Assign tasks to a specific agent. Let an orchestrator choose the best agent or group of agents for a task. Connect agents so one agent’s output becomes another agent’s input. Track the progress and results of each workflow. Give agents feedback that can improve future tasks. Generate both text and images. In a multi-agent workflow, each agent completes part of the task and passes its work to the next agent. This allows each specialist to build on the work completed before them. How we built it We built the frontend using React and Vite . The application includes pages for onboarding, agent management, advanced settings, task creation, progress tracking, and feedback. The backend uses Node.js and Express . It handles creating and updating agents, managing tasks, generating teams, improving instructions, and turning feedback into reusable context. We used the Google Gemini API to: Select the best agent for a task. Create multi-agent workflows. Generate responses from specialized agents. Suggest an AI team based on a business description. Improve task prompts and agent instructions. Recommend context updates based on user feedback. Agents can depend on one another, so Bullpen makes sure they run in the correct order and prevents circular workflows. We also used Google Imagen for agents that generate images. Agent and task data is stored in Upstash Redis , allowing the information to remain available across Vercel’s serverless functions. The complete application is deployed through Vercel . Challenges we ran into One of our biggest challenges was multi-agent orchestration. Bullpen needed to: Understand the user’s task. Select the correct agent or agents. Determine the order in which the agents should work. Pass results between agents. Display progress to the user. Serverless storage was another challenge. Our original in-memory storage worked locally, but data could disappear when Vercel sent requests to different serverless instances. We solved this by moving agent and task data into Upstash Redis . We also experienced differences between local Express routing and Vercel’s production routing. Some endpoints initially returned 404 Not Found errors. We fixed this by creating specific serverless entry points for those routes. Another challenge was model availability. Some Gemini model names that previously worked were not available for newer API keys. We tested the available models and updated Bullpen to use supported alternatives. Finally, we worked to make a complicated AI system feel simple. Instead of showing users dependency graphs and technical functions, Bullpen presents agents as employees, instructions as responsibilities, and the orchestrator as a manager. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Bullpen is more than a collection of separate chatbots. Its agents can work together through connected workflows and build on one another’s results. We are especially proud of: Building a working multi-agent orchestration system. Supporting custom instructions, models, context, and specialties for each agent. Automatically creating a suggested team based on a user’s business. Allowing feedback to improve an agent’s future behavior. Storing agent and task data in a serverless environment. Supporting both text and image generation. Creating a polished interface that makes advanced AI concepts easier to understand. Building and deploying the project within a limited hackathon timeframe. What we learned We learned that building a reliable AI product requires more than sending a prompt to a model. Storage, validation, orchestration, routing, error handling, and user experience are just as important as the generated response. We also learned that serverless systems must be designed around stateless execution. Any information that needs to remain available between requests must be stored outside an individual serverless function. Most importantly, we learned that complicated AI systems are easier to understand when they are presented through a familiar idea. Users do not need to understand dependency graphs or technical workflows. They can simply build a team, assign work, and review the results. What's next for Bullpen Next, we want to expand Bullpen with: User accounts and separate workspaces. Integrations with email, calendars, cloud storage, and business tools. Scheduled and recurring tasks. Shared organizational knowledge. Agent performance analytics. Version history for agent instructions and context. Human approval steps inside workflows. Parallel execution for agents that can work independently. More reliable processing for long-running tasks. Our long-term vision is for Bullpen to become a complete workspace where anyone can build, manage, and continuously improve their own AI team.

title: Chronos — Legacy Code Archaeologist
tagline: Upload any ancient codebase. Get an AI-powered dependency map, plain-English excavation report, and a full TypeScript refactor — in minutes, not months.
description: Chronos — Legacy Code Archaeologist Inspiration It was 2 AM on a Tuesday when I first truly understood the problem. A senior engineer at a fintech company — someone with 15 years of experience — was staring at a single Java file. 4,000 lines long. No comments. Variable names like x2 , tmpVal , and doTheThing() . He had been staring at it for three days. His job was to add a single field to a form. One field. Three days. Because nobody knew what that file touched. The engineer who wrote it? Left in 2011. His name was Dave. Every engineering team has a Dave file. A file that only Dave understood — and Dave left years ago. Nobody touches it. Nobody documents it. It just sits there, costing the company money every single day while engineers work around it like a landmine. We didn't invent this problem. $4 trillion in COBOL transactions are processed every 24 hours. 95% of ATM withdrawals worldwide run on code written before most of us were born. Enterprises spend 74% more of their maintenance budget on legacy systems than on building new ones. The standard solution? Hire consultants for 18 months just to understand the system before writing a single line of new code. Current tools give you a report. A list of warnings. Code smells. "That's not archaeology — that's a receipt." We wanted to build the excavator. So we built Chronos. What it does Chronos is an AI-powered legacy code intelligence platform that turns an incomprehensible, undocumented codebase into a living, navigable map — in minutes, not months. You drop in any legacy codebase — COBOL, ancient Java, C, PHP, anything — and Chronos gives you five things that previously didn't exist in a single tool: 1. Interactive Dependency Graph A real-time force-directed visualization of every file, module, and relationship in your codebase. Node size reflects lines of code. Red nodes are danger zones — high coupling, high risk. Click any node and watch every dependency light up instantly. For the first time, you can see what connects to what. 2. AI Excavation Report Claude reads your entire codebase and produces a plain-English intelligence briefing : what the system actually does, what architecture pattern it follows, which five files are the load-bearing walls, and what the overall tech debt score is. What used to take senior engineers months now takes 40 seconds. 3. Dependency Map Analysis Claude identifies circular dependencies, god classes , dead code candidates, and tightly coupled modules — then produces a prioritized refactoring roadmap so your team knows exactly where to start, instead of guessing blind. 4. Refactor Blueprint Select any file. Chronos produces a line-by-line plain-English explanation of what the legacy code actually does , followed by a full production-ready rewrite in modern TypeScript or Python — complete with a side-by-side diff view and migration risk notes. Dave's file. Finally understood. 5. Archaeology Terminal A CLI interface where engineers can run commands like scan --deep , risk-score , refactor [filename] , and deps --outdated — and Gemini responds as if executing real operations on the codebase. For the engineers who live in the terminal and trust nothing they can't type themselves. How we built it Chronos is a nextjs application — built around three core layers working in concert: The Brain — Gemini API Gemini is the reasoning engine. We didn't just call the API — we engineered it. Every analysis tab sends carefully crafted prompts built around a system prompt that gives Gemini the persona of a 30-year enterprise modernization veteran , not a generic code assistant. The difference in output quality between a generic prompt and a persona-driven one was not marginal — it was categorical. We implemented streaming via the Anthropic Messages API so output renders as a live typewriter effect — making the AI reasoning feel alive, not like a loading spinner staring back at you. The Map — D3.js v7 D3 powers the force-directed dependency graph. Nodes are sized by lines of code, colored by language, and flagged red when coupling exceeds risk thresholds. Edges animate like electrical signals traveling along wires when a node is selected. We implemented zoom, pan, clustering toggle, and a minimap — all rendered at 60fps. The Upload Layer — JSZip JSZip handles .zip codebase uploads entirely on the client side — language detection, file manifest generation, and automatic LOC counting — before a single API call is made. No unnecessary data transfer. No waiting. The Demo Mode We built a realistic 47-file legacy Java banking system — complete with god classes, circular dependencies, and dead code clusters — so any judge or user can explore every feature of Chronos without uploading a real codebase. A tool lives or dies on its first five minutes. We made those five minutes count. Challenges we ran into Context Architecture for Large Codebases A real 50,000-file monolith cannot fit in a single API call. We designed an intelligent chunking and prioritization strategy — sending Gemini the file manifest plus representative samples from the highest-risk, most-connected nodes, rather than brute-forcing the full codebase. Getting Claude to reason about cross-file relationships from partial context took significant iteration to get right. Prompt Engineering for Faithful Refactoring Getting Gemini to produce a TypeScript rewrite that is semantically faithful to ancient COBOL business logic — not just syntactically correct — required a very specific system prompt. Generic "rewrite this in TypeScript" prompts produced clean code that missed the actual intent entirely. The archaeologist persona and explicit migration risk instructions made a measurable difference in output quality. Graph Performance at Scale D3 force simulations with 200+ nodes and 400+ edges can destroy frame rate fast. We tuned the simulation alpha decay, collision radii, and link distance parameters to keep the graph fluid without sacrificing visual accuracy. Getting to 60fps on the demo codebase required three full rewrites of the simulation config. Making Streaming Feel Intentional Streaming from the Anthropic API is fast — but unstructured fast output feels chaotic. We added structured section headers in the system prompt so Gemini always produces ASCII-divided sections, turning the typewriter output into something that feels like a real intelligence report being written live, not a token flood. Accomplishments that we're proud of We're proud that Gemini doesn't feel like a hackathon project — it feels like a product. The boot sequence. The terminal easter egg. The animated graph edges. The streaming report. Every detail was intentional , because we believed that if the experience didn't feel polished, judges would never trust the intelligence behind it. More specifically: the Refactor Blueprint tab produces output that is genuinely useful. We tested it against real legacy Java snippets pulled from open-source repositories — and the TypeScript rewrites were production-quality, not toy examples. That's the Gemini edge working exactly as intended. And the demo mode. We are most proud of the demo mode. Building a realistic 47-file banking system — with real dependency patterns, real god classes, real circular dependencies — means any judge can experience the full depth of Gemini in under five minutes without needing to find a legacy codebase first. Show, don't tell. What we learned Gemini's reasoning across multiple files is genuinely different from other models — not marginally, but categorically. The ability to hold cross-file relationships in context while simultaneously reasoning about business logic intent is what makes the Refactor Blueprint work. You cannot fake this with a smaller context window. It is the architectural foundation everything else is built on. We also learned that prompt persona matters enormously. "Senior software engineer" and "30-year legacy modernization archaeologist" produce measurably different outputs on the same exact input. The model's frame of reference shapes its reasoning. This alone changed how we think about prompt engineering forever. On the product side: the biggest insight was that the visualization layer is what unlocks trust. Engineers don't act on AI recommendations they can't verify. But when they can see the dependency graph and confirm that the god class Gemini flagged is actually connected to 31 files — the trust threshold for acting on the refactor blueprint drops dramatically. Show before tell. Always. What's next for Chronos — Legacy Code Archaeologist The current terminal is a simulation — Gemini reasons about what commands would find. The next version integrates Gemini Code's CLI agent so Chronos actually executes operations in a sandboxed environment: running tests, identifying failing dependencies, applying refactors to real files. That's when Chronos stops being an intelligence tool and becomes a true autonomous modernization agent. Beyond that: GitHub & GitLab direct integration — point Chronos at a repository URL, no upload needed Tech debt scoring dashboard — track improvement over time as the team refactors, sprint by sprint Enterprise version — role-based access, audit trails, and on-premise deployment for regulated industries: banks, insurance companies, government systems — the exact organizations drowning in legacy code and legally unable to send it to cloud AI tools today The Dave file problem is everywhere. We're just getting started. Built with Claude API · claude-sonnet-4-20250514 · JavaScript · D3.js v7 · JSZip · Highlight.js · HTML5 · ` · Anthropic Streaming API`

title: Doom Fitness

description: GIF Visual footage Inspiration A major portion of our generation is constantly scrolling on social media, which hinders their productivity. This app's purpose is to fix that, and provide a users an easy way to be active at the same time. What It Does After a certain amount of time scrolling on the same site, the doom countdown will start, and then the user will be required to complete 5 squats or 5 jumping jacks on camera to unlock their ability to scroll again. After the user has spent some more time scrolling, the countdown shows up again, and the cycle repeats. How We Built It We used TensorFlow.js to locate the 17 main body points on camera. We then measured the distance between the different body points and compared the distances to ensure that the user was doing the correct exercises. Using the Manifest V3 extension, when the limit was reached, a flag was activated in Chrome storage and background service workers to prohibit entry to a blocked site. What We Learned We learned that the permission a browser features has to pass through page policy, extension, and the OS before a webcam can even be turned on. Also, sometimes simple math instead of heavy AI recognition can be used as long as the measurements are good. title: CareFlow
tagline: A linked-list-based ER queue system that automatically prioritizes patients by severity, age, pain level, and wait time; so, the most critical patients are always seen first.
description: Inspiration Emergency rooms often operate on a first-come, first-served basis, which doesn't reflect medical urgency. A patient with a minor complaint who arrives first can end up being seen before someone with a life-threatening condition who arrives later. We wanted to build a system that mirrors how real triage should work prioritizing patients based on how critical their condition is, not just when they walked in. What it does CareFlow is a patient queue management system for emergency rooms. It lets staff add patients with their age, pain level, and severity, and automatically calculates a priority score for each one. Patients are queued so the most urgent cases are seen first. The system also lets staff search for and update a patient's information, view the full waitlist, pull statistics on how many patients are critical/urgent/non-urgent, and call the next patient in line. How we built it We built CareFlow in C, using a singly linked list to represent the ER queue, where the list stays sorted by priority score as patients are added. Each patient node stores their name, age, pain level, severity, computed priority score, and arrival time. Priority scores are calculated using a weighted formula that factors in severity, age, and pain level, and can be recalculated over time to account for how long a patient has been waiting. Challenges we ran into Managing dynamic memory correctly was one of our biggest challenges — particularly making sure patient names (stored as dynamically allocated strings) were properly freed and reallocated whenever a patient's information was edited, to avoid memory leaks. We also had to think carefully about maintaining sorted order in the linked list every time a new patient was inserted, rather than sorting after the fact. Accomplishments that we're proud of We're proud of building a fully functional priority queue from scratch using core data structures, without relying on any external libraries. We're especially proud of the priority recalculation logic, which factors in wait time so patients don't get stuck waiting indefinitely behind higher-severity cases. What we learned We deepened our understanding of linked list manipulation, pointer-to-pointer parameters for modifying list heads, and safe dynamic memory management in C. We also learned how to translate a real-world process (ER triage) into a working prioritization algorithm. What's next for CareFlow Next steps include adding a graphical interface, persistent storage (saving patient data between sessions), and more sophisticated priority weighting that could incorporate additional medical factors or be configurable per hospital.

title: FormCheck
tagline: Physical Therapy brought to the palm of your hand.
description: Inspiration I was inspired to take on this project as I have struggled with chronic knee pain for the last 5 years of my life, with tendinitis in both knees. I have gone to physical therapy multiple times, and while it has been productive, someone cannot be there to constantly judge my form and give me feedback for exercises to prevent re-injury. Squatting is something in particular that has been challenging for me, which is where I was inspired to start this project. I wanted to build something real, that would benefit me and potentially others in everyday life beyond just this hackathon. What it does FormCheck is an AI fitness trainer that uses a smart bracelet and computer vision to analyze real time movements and gives constructive, personalized feedbacks on your workouts. The user wears the smart bracelet and a camera which track movements and stability. After completing a set, the AI fitness trainer gives feedback on which parts of that set were good and what can be worked on. The user can also give the trainer points of interest to focus on, such as knee stability, and give feedback based on those provided comments. How we built it Hardware Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32-S3(MPU) HiLetgo GY-521(IMU) AKZYTUE 3.7V 400mAh LiPo Battery Logitech Brio 100 Webcam Nylon Webbing Software Onshape Python VScode Arduino Google Gemini API MediaPipe Challenges we ran into Hardware Challenges Post print design issues Physical port connection Solder joints Software Challenges Rate limit on Free Tier Gemini Knee Angle Tracking on Side Profile Coach AI Misread Rep Scoring Software Tuning ## Accomplishments that we're proud of Built a fully working end-to-end pipeline, CV-> scoring-> wearable-> Ai Coaching Designed a scoring system that's rule-based and explainable Successfully integrated two competing signal sources (camera + wearable) ## What we learned Rule based scoring needs more than just intuition, and requires multiple trial runs and data in order to accurately tune. What's next for FormCheck Next on FormCheck is improving Quality of Life features, such as: More Secure Lid Waterproof Simple Wristband Adjustment Create Designated LiPo Containment Support for additional exercises beyond squats Native Phone App On device local inference- privacy first approach for personal fitness.

title: Lumen
tagline: Turning confusing door-to-door solar pitches and fine print contracts into clear data, helping homeowners spot hidden red flags, uncover scams, and easily compare quotes.
description: We’ve all heard stories—or experienced it firsthand—where a door-to-door sales rep pitches a "free" or "low-cost" solar installation, talks fast, and leaves behind a dense 30-page contract locking homeowners into financial agreements. We built Lumen to create a transparent, leveling playing field for both sides. For homeowners, Lumen acts as a smart assistant that breaks down dense PDF contracts into clear summaries, pointing out hidden clauses and benchmarking quotes. For installers, it's powerful tool for empathy and transparency—giving them a clear view of how their offer actually lands and letting them prove on the spot that their deal is fair and trustworthy.

title: DayList
tagline: Most playlist apps ask what music you want to hear. DayList asks how your day felt, then creates a soundtrack and a lyric that captures that moment.
description: Inspiration Music can capture many moments and moods of everyday life, from small moments such as coffee days and morning walks to bigger events such as weddings, graduations and even concerts. The idea of creating a music app to help capture these moments in songs and/or playlists came from a hackathon idea on ChatGPT, and from then on, DayList came to life. What it does DayList is an app that can generate playlists and song recommendations based on certain events of the day prompted by the user. How it works is that the user will go on DayList app; log into Spotify and then be redirected to DayList to prompt some events of their day. DayList will then generate the prompt using Gemini API to suggest five songs based on the mood of the day. How we built it We used React for the frontend, and integrated Spotify API for login purposes and the Gemini API for generating the songs and captions and moods for the prompted events. Challenges we ran into Two of the biggest challenges we ran into were connecting the frontend and backends for DayList, as well as integrating the Spotify and Gemini APIs with each other. Accomplishments that we're proud of We successfully got the APIs working with each other for backend and connected the backend to the frontend. What we learned We learned a lot about how to implement backend technologies such as Spotify and Gemini APIs into DayList and how to integrate the backend with the React frontend code. What's next for DayList We were going to incorporate the photo uploading feature into DayList, but unfortunately due to time constraints and problems with the backend, we did not get there in time. I think I could handle that on my own if I get time.

description: Project Inspiration We loved tomodachi life for the switch so we tried to bring a little bit of its magic onto web! What it does You make a character (called a "Wheez") and take care of them! How we built it React NodeJS, Firebase Hosting Challenges we ran into Integrating Live2D into the website. title: WhoOwnsIt
tagline: WhoOwnsIt lets you scan any product to reveal its parent company, stock info, and what monthly investing in that company could have returned.
description: Landing Page Stock Information Page Inspiration We wanted to make financial literacy feel immediate and personal. Most people interact with public companies every day through snacks, clothes, phones, and household products, but they rarely know who actually owns those brands. WhoOwnsIt turns everyday objects into an entry point for understanding markets. What it does WhoOwnsIt lets users upload or scan a product image, identifies the brand, traces the corporate ownership chain, and shows the ultimate parent company. If that parent is a U.S.-listed public company, the app shows stock data, a one-year chart, and a calculator showing what monthly investing in that company could have returned. How we built it We built the frontend with React and Vite, using a simple scan-to-result flow. The backend uses Express and calls Gemini to identify products and reason through ownership. Financial Modeling Prep provides company and stock data, while cached mock data keeps the demo reliable. The DCA calculator uses a shared formula on both client and server so slider updates can happen instantly. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was handling ownership correctly. Products can be licensed, privately owned, foreign-owned, or part of complex parent-company structures. We also had to keep the app reliable when APIs or keys were unavailable, so mock mode and caching became important parts of the architecture. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud of turning a product photo into a full ownership and investing story. The project connects computer vision, company research, financial data, and a clean user experience into one simple flow. We are also proud that it handles non-public and foreign companies honestly instead of forcing every product into a stock chart. What we learned We learned how important clear API contracts are when frontend and backend work happen in parallel. We also learned that financial apps need careful edge-case handling, especially around ticker validation, corporate ownership, and investment disclaimers. Most of all, we learned that everyday objects can be a surprisingly powerful way to explain markets. What's next for WhoOwnsIt Next, we want to polish the result screens, improve the ownership visuals, expand demo coverage, and strengthen the product-identification prompts. We also want to add more educational context so users understand not just who owns a product, but how that company fits into the larger market.

title: EcoCart AI
tagline: AI-powered receipt analyzer for smarter, more sustainable shopping.
description: Inspiration: Every shopping trip has an environmental impact, but most people never see it. While nutrition labels help us understand the health impact of our food, there is no simple way to understand the sustainability impact of everyday purchases. We wanted to build a tool that makes environmental awareness as easy as scanning a receipt. Instead of asking people to change their habits overnight, EcoCart AI helps them make small, practical improvements that add up over time. What it Does: EcoCart AI is an AI-powered receipt analyzer that transforms grocery receipts into personalized sustainability reports. Users simply upload a receipt, and the application: Extracts purchased items using AI vision Calculates a sustainability (carbon) score Identifies high-impact purchases Recommends greener alternatives Estimates potential environmental and financial savings Tracks progress across previous receipts Awards achievements and weekly sustainability challenges The goal is to encourage smarter shopping through simple, actionable insights rather than overwhelming statistics. How I Built It: I built EcoCart AI using modern web technologies and AI. Frontend: React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS AI: OpenAI Vision (GPT-5 mini) for receipt understanding EcoCart AI lets users upload a grocery receipt and instantly receive a personalized sustainability report. It analyzes the items, calculates a carbon score, highlights high-impact purchases, suggests greener alternatives, provides AI-powered shopping tips, tracks progress over time, and rewards users with fun achievements and weekly challenges to encourage more sustainable shopping habits. One of the biggest challenges was making the experience feel useful instead of overwhelming. I also worked on: Designing a scoring system that is easy to understand Presenting environmental data in a simple and motivating way Generating realistic recommendations rather than generic advice Creating a clean, startup-style interface suitable for everyday users Comparing multiple receipts to show measurable improvement over time Another challenge was ensuring the AI produced consistent, believable sustainability recommendations while keeping the interface fast and intuitive. What We Learned This project taught us that AI can do much more than answer questions—it can help people make better everyday decisions. I also gained experience with: Building AI-powered user experiences Prompt engineering AI vision for document understanding Designing sustainable technology products Creating intuitive dashboards for complex information Future Improvements I plan to expand EcoCart AI with: Barcode scanning for individual products Personalized shopping recommendations Store-specific sustainability comparisons Household sustainability tracking Monthly environmental reports Integration with grocery retailers and loyalty programs Why EcoCart AI Matters: Small shopping decisions happen every day. If millions of people could instantly understand the environmental impact of their purchases, they could make better choices without changing their lifestyle dramatically. EcoCart AI turns an ordinary receipt into an opportunity to build healthier habits—for both people and the planet. 🌎💚

title: Usaid
tagline: Experience the future before you choose it
description: GIF Inspiration As humans, we are bad at long-term decision-making. We underestimate risks, overestimate our future motivation, and often ignore the second-order effects of our choices. Whether it's quitting a job, moving to a new country, or starting a company, we're forced to make life-altering decisions based on gut feelings and limited data. We realized that while there are tools to track tasks and games to simulate fantasy worlds, there was nothing to simulate your own future . What if decision-making was like a video game? What if you could "save your game," try a risky path, see the consequences, and then rewind if it didn't work out? This inspired Usaid , a cognitive time simulator that brings the power of "Scenario Planning" (used by military and corporate strategists) to personal life decisions. What it does Usaid is an AI-powered engine that generates multiple, distinct future timelines based on a single real-world decision. You enter a dilemma (e.g., "Should I quit my job to start a startup?"). Usaid analyzes your profile (risk tolerance, values, current state) and generates few feasible divergent future paths (Optimistic, Pragmatic, Remote/Risky). Each timeline is visualized with year-by-year events and quantifiable metrics for Career, Finance, Relationships, and Mental Wellbeing. You can "inject" new decisions into any timeline (e.g., "What if I get funding in Year 2?") and watch the future rewrite itself in real-time. It’s not just advice.. it’s experiential foresight of once own life. How it is built Usaid is a modern full-stack application leveraging the latest in Generative AI. The AI Engine: Google Gemini 3's advanced reasoning capabilities has been used to build the simulation core. Prompt Engineering is been used to build something beyond simple text generation by constructing a persistent "Cognitive State Model" for the user. The Frontend: Built with React, TypeScript, and Vite, featuring a premium "Glassmorphism" UI. Framer Motion is used for smooth timeline animations and Chart.js (or similar visualization libs) to make the data tangible. The Backend: A robust Node.js/Express server that acts as the orchestrator. It handles authentication, manages the SQLite database (via Prisma), and streams AI responses to the client. The Design: Heavy focus on "Industrial Polish", using a dark, futuristic aesthetic with neon accents to make the user feel like they are stepping into a control room for their life. Challenges we ran into Hallucination Control: Getting an LLM to consistently generate plausible 5-year timelines without veering into fantasy was tough. Strict schema validation implementation and "Chain-of-Thought" prompting helps a lot. Latency: Simulating 5 concurrent futures is computationally expensive. Gemini 3 Flash know for its flash speed has been used and a streaming architecture has been implemented so users see the first timeline immediately while the others generate in the background. Visualizing Abstract Data: How do you visualize "Emotional Wellbeing" over 5 years? The UI has been iterated multiple times to find a graphical representation that was intuitive but not overwhelming. Accomplishments that make me proud The "Wow" Factor: The moment you see your life split into three different paths on the screen is genuinely powerful. Structured AI: I managed to tame a creative LLM into outputting complex, mathematically consistent graph data. The UI: The interface feels incredibly premium and responsive. It doesn't feel like a hackathon project, it feels like a SaaS product. What I learned Gemini 3 is a Reasoner, not just a Writer: If we give Gemini enough context about a user's psychology, it can predict second-order effects (e.g., "High career growth = Risk of burnout/divorce") with scary accuracy. The Power of Context: The quality of the simulation is directly proportional to how much the AI knows about the user. Personalization is the key. What's next for Usaid Reality Feedback Loop: Allowing users to log what actually happened, so the system learns from reality and improves its future predictions. Multi-Agent Extensions: Adding specific AI advisors (a "Risk Manager," a "Career Coach," a "Therapist") who debate the pros and cons of your timelines. Scientific Extensions: Applying the same engine to simulate research paths or startup pivots for teams.

title: KnightQuest
tagline: KnightQuest turns exploring UCF's campus into a role-playing game — students earn XP, titles, and gear by completing real quests at real campus buildings.
description: Inspiration Every fall, thousands of new Knights show up on UCF's campus and have no idea where anything is — the Library gets confused with the Union, Engineering I feels like a maze, and orientation week is a blur of building names nobody remembers. We wanted campus exploration to feel less like a checklist and more like something students would actually want to do. RPGs have spent decades turning "go talk to the guy in the tower" into something compelling — we figured campus navigation deserved the same treatment. What it does KnightQuest turns the UCF campus into a fantasy realm. Students create a character — name, major, personality — and are dropped onto an interactive map of real campus buildings, each reskinned as a quest location (Millican Hall is "The Gate," the Student Union is "The Tavern," Towers Dorms is "The Keep"). Clicking a building launches a quest: complete it by snapping a photo on location or answering a trivia question about that building. Completing quests earns XP, unlocks inventory items, and levels the player up through titles — Squire, Knight, Champion, and beyond. A "Campus Oracle" narrates the journey with flavor text, achievements pop as milestones are hit, and a quest log keeps track of what's done and what's left across all 8 locations. How we built it The whole experience runs as a single self-contained HTML/CSS/JS app — no build step, no backend required to demo. The campus map is hand-built as an SVG with building nodes connected by paths, styled to feel like a fantasy region map rather than a literal campus map. Game state (XP, inventory, completed quests, achievements) lives in-memory and drives a small state machine that updates the player card, XP bar, and quest log in real time. The "Oracle" text uses a typewriter effect for narrative flavor, and a Demo Mode toggle lets quests be completed instantly (bypassing photo/trivia requirements) for fast walkthroughs and presentations. Challenges we ran into Getting the layout to hold up across screen sizes was trickier than expected — a full-viewport, no-scroll game UI looks great on one screen size and completely breaks on another. We hit a subtle CSS bug where the sidebar and main content area were being vertically centered instead of stretched, which pushed key UI (like the Oracle panel) off-screen entirely on certain desktop window sizes — a bug that was especially annoying because it only showed up at some resolutions and not others. Balancing "no-scroll, everything visible at once" against "works on a phone" also took a few iterations before we landed on letting each screen scroll gracefully instead of forcing everything to fit. Accomplishments that we're proud of A fully playable loop — character creation, quests, XP, leveling, achievements — built without any external backend. A campus map that actually feels like a game world instead of a literal Google Maps screenshot. Flexible quest verification (photo proof or trivia) so the game works whether or not a player is physically on campus. A Demo Mode that makes the whole experience presentable in under a minute for judges, without faking the underlying mechanics. What we learned Small UI details — a typing animation, a level-up flash, a toast notification — do a lot of heavy lifting in making a static form-and-button app feel like a game. We also learned firsthand how deceptively fragile "fill the whole screen, no scrolling" layouts are, and how much more resilient the app became once we let content scroll instead of forcing it to fit. What's next for KnightQuest Real GPS verification so photo proof requires actually being at the building. Multiplayer leaderboards across dorms, majors, or orientation groups. More building quests covering the full UCF campus, plus seasonal/event-based limited quests. A lightweight backend so progress persists across devices and sessions instead of resetting per browser.

title: Kaleidoscope
tagline: An alt data terminal to predict retailers' stock value.
description: Walmart - Summary Walmart - Satellite Pricing Inspiration Our team was inspired by the idea that real-world activity can reveal valuable insights before they appear in traditional financial reports. Supply chains, satellite images, and public search behavior all tell a story about a company’s momentum; however, these signals are rarely analyzed together. Therefore, Kaleidoscope was created to bring these scattered signals together and provide a clearer, data-driven view of company confidence. What it does Kaleidoscope is an alternative data intelligence platform that analyzes companies using multiple public data sources. It tracks import activity and supply chain movement, detects changes in physical operations and locations, and measures public interest and market attention. Our website processes these signals and generates a company confidence score, helping users quickly understand potential growth, changes, and trends beyond traditional financial data. How we built it Kaleidoscope runs on data stored in a Turso database. Multiple public APIs feed information, which is processed by a Python script that keeps certain data cached for easy retrieval. Other widgets update live, such as the Gemini report. Challenges we ran into Integrating multiple data sources: each API and dataset had different formats, limitations, and reliability challenges. Data availability and consistency: finding clean, usable public data and handling missing information required additional processing. Building a meaningful confidence score: combining different signals into one score required balancing multiple factors while keeping results understandable. As our team worked under a limited hackathon timeline, we had to prioritize core features and build a functional prototype quickly. Accomplishments that we are proud of We built a working alternative data intelligence platform from scratch during the hackathon. We successfully connected multiple public signals into a unified company analysis pipeline. We demonstrated how non-traditional data sources can provide valuable insights beyond financial reports. We collaborated as a team to design, develop, and deploy a complete application. What we learned Real-world data is messy and requires strong validation and fallback strategies. Combining different data sources can reveal insights that individual sources cannot provide alone. Building a useful product requires balancing technical complexity with user experience. Rapid prototyping and communication are critical when developing under time constraints. What is next for Kaleidoscope Improve the confidence scoring model with machine learning techniques. Build a more advanced platform for analysts, investors, and businesses. Provide historical tracking to identify changes in company momentum over time. So please stay tuned, and support to view the details of more retailers is the next step in sight.

title: MarketSphere
tagline: Ditch the dreadful spreadsheets and endless article scrolling. Spin the globe instead — MarketSphere turns global markets into a living 3D world you explore, not scroll through.
description: Welcome Page Choosing North America View Choosing Europe View Choosing Asia View Inspiration We were inspired by the Bloomberg Terminal the industry standard, all-in-one command center that lets Wall Street traders see the entire world's markets and news at a glance. It's an incredible tool, but it's average price is $30,000/year and has a UI built for professionals who already know exactly what they're looking for. We wanted to bring that same Bloomberg-style, world-view terminal experience to the everyday retail investor instead. That idea became MarketSphere: an interactive 3D globe as your world-view terminal, where spinning to any region surfaces its live markets and news. To help users actually navigate and interpret all of it, we paired the globe with a Gemini-powered LLM assistant grounded in live news and financial data. Ask it a question about what you're looking at and it answers in that context, or ask it, in natural language, to build you a dynamic panel of markets and news on the fly, completely controlled by you. What it does MarketSphere is a full-screen interactive 3D globe as your market dashboard. Spin it, click a continent, and the camera swoops in while a live panel slides out with real candlestick charts (yfinance OHLCV, rendered on our own chart) and real news headlines pulled from GDELT, the Guardian, and Alpha Vantage. A Gemini-powered chat assistant lives in in the browser, ask it a question and it gives you an answer grounded in live data, ask it to build something and it assembles a custom workspace on the fly, or ask it to analyze a company and it hands back a real price-vs-narrative analysis. How we built it Next.js/TypeScript frontend with react-globe.gl + three.js driving the globe, Framer Motion for the camera/panel choreography, and TradingView's open-source Lightweight Charts for the market panel. FastAPI + Postgres backend, with a news ingestion pipeline pulling from three sources and a Gemini-backed router that classifies each chat message into answer / build / analyze before responding. Challenges we ran into We're especially proud of the AI copilot experience. Rather than acting as a generic chatbot, here Gemini is grounded in whatever the user is actively exploring on the platform. They help interpret the signals, explain what the data means, surface relevant context, and answer questions in the specific market and news context the user is viewing. What we learned We improved our ability to scope projects by turning large goals into actionable steps, prioritizing tasks, and iterating through smaller milestones instead of trying to solve everything at once. This approach helped us stay organized, identify issues earlier, and build more efficiently as a team. What's next for MarketSphere Country/state-level scope selection, a real tone-vs-price overlay directly on the chart (the data model supports it, the UI doesn't yet), persisting chat-built workspaces, and widening news source coverage beyond the current three. Also, we hope AI copilot interaction can change UI is relation to what user asks.

title: WakeForce – Your Ultimate Awakening Companion

description: WakeForce helps users build better mornings with smart alarms, interactive missions, streak tracking, and habit analytics. Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for WakeForce – Your Ultimate Awakening Companion Inspiration Many people struggle to wake up on time because traditional alarm clocks are easy to snooze or ignore. title: Solar-Sanity Check
tagline: Easy to see how and if solar panels are right for you using Google Solar API and Gemni.
description: Roof side Money side Inspiration My family has been talking about adding solar panels for years but aren't sure about the cost or where they should go. I thought this project might provide a solution to that kind of problem. What it does It takes in a users address, electric bill, and solar quote, and uses those inputs to determine if a user should get solar panels at all, and if they do, where those panels should go on the roof and what pricing they should be striving for. How we built it First I added the Solar and Gemni API keys, then I started the basics of the financial side, using a Solar API call to determine whether or not a user should get solar panels or not based off how much the sun hit their roof. After that I added Gemni calls to get the users electric bill and solar quote and analyze them/use them to determine whether solar panels were worth the cost at all. After that I added the roof designer, which was made from adding the Maps Static API get satellite images of houses and Geocaching API to switch between those images to show houses all around the world. After that I added the optional solar panels on the pictures, using the Solar API to determine the best possible placement of the solar panels on the roofs. Challenges we ran into The API keys would be an issue frequently as billing was required so I had to learn how to navigate Google Cloud and make sure my API keys were secure as well as my billing account worked and wouldn't overcharge me if anything. What we learned A lot about Google APIs and mapping, that was the big thing that I hadn't done too much of before this hackathon. title: PlantPilot
tagline: Plants are living systems and their own caretakers. We built an AI-powered plant caregiver that uses computer vision to understand a plant's condition and respond by delivering water when needed.
description: Using a standard webcam, our system uses computer vision and AI to analyze a plant’s appearance, identify signs of stress, and determine when watering is needed. The AI assistant interacts with users through a chat interface, explains the plant’s condition, and can autonomously trigger a physical watering mechanism. A MacBook serves as the intelligence hub, processing the camera feed and sending commands through USB to an ESP32 microcontroller. The ESP32 controls an RC-based robotic mechanism that activates a spray bottle, creating a low-cost prototype of an intelligent agricultural system. By combining AI perception, conversational interaction, and physical automation, our project demonstrates how future farming systems can become adaptive, responsive, and personalized to individual plant needs.

title: review-geniee
tagline: ReviewGenie helps businesses collect more authentic reviews through QR codes and uses AI to analyze customer feedback, turning reviews into actionable business insights.
description: ReviewGenie Inspiration Online reviews have become one of the biggest factors influencing customer decisions, yet collecting them is still surprisingly difficult. Customers often intend to leave a review but abandon the process because they need to search for the business on Google or another platform. At the same time, businesses receive reviews but rarely have the time or tools to understand what customers are actually saying. We wanted to solve both problems with one product: make leaving reviews effortless while transforming customer feedback into actionable insights. What it does ReviewGenie helps businesses collect more authentic customer reviews through a unique QR code. Customers simply scan the QR code and are taken directly to the business's review page, removing unnecessary friction from the review process. Once reviews are collected, AI analyzes the feedback to identify customer sentiment, recurring issues, common compliments, and emerging trends. Business owners can view these insights in a real-time dashboard, helping them understand what customers love and where improvements are needed. How we built it The application combines a modern web interface with AI-powered analytics. Key components include: Secure authentication for business accounts QR code generation for review collection Review management dashboard AI-powered sentiment analysis Business analytics and visual insights Responsive UI supporting desktop and mobile devices The architecture was designed to keep review collection simple while providing meaningful insights through AI. Challenges we ran into One of the biggest challenges was designing a review flow that remained simple for customers while still giving businesses valuable analytics. Another challenge was converting unstructured review text into useful insights. We focused on extracting meaningful sentiment and recurring themes instead of simply displaying raw reviews. We also spent considerable time refining the user experience to ensure every step—from generating a QR code to viewing analytics—was intuitive and required minimal effort. What we learned This project reinforced that solving a real business problem is more valuable than adding unnecessary features. We also gained experience integrating AI into a practical workflow, designing user-centered interfaces, and building dashboards that transform raw data into actionable information. Most importantly, we learned that AI delivers the greatest value when it helps users make better decisions rather than simply automating tasks. What's next for ReviewGenie Our vision is to make ReviewGenie an AI-powered customer feedback platform for businesses of every size. Future plans include: Multi-platform review aggregation AI-generated response suggestions Competitor review benchmarking Customer satisfaction trend prediction Team collaboration and role management Automated business reports and recommendations Our long-term goal is to help businesses not only collect more reviews but continuously improve customer experience through AI-driven insights.

title: Jeans that Fit!

title: Trade Coach, Personalized Instant Journal Analyzer
tagline: Paste your trade history, get an instant AI coaching summary that spots your costly patterns before they cost you more.
description: Inspiration I'm an economics student who's been building my own trading tools — a position-size calculator, a growth simulator, a manual trade journal — while learning forex and crypto trading. The thing I kept running into was simple: I could log my trades, but I couldn't actually see the patterns in them. I knew I had a discipline problem somewhere in my losses, but spotting it by scrolling through rows in a spreadsheet never worked. I wanted my own journal to talk back to me. What it does Trade Coach takes your trade history — date, pair, direction, entry/exit price, size, P&L, and your own notes — and turns it into an honest coaching report: Pattern detection — automatically flags revenge trading after losses, stop-loss discipline issues, and losing streaks, pulled straight from your notes and numbers. An equity curve — a live chart of your account's cumulative performance, trade by trade. Kelly-fraction position sizing — calculates what fraction of your account your own win rate and reward:risk ratio actually justify risking per trade, plus a safer half-Kelly recommendation. Risk-of-ruin estimate — a probability of blowing the account if current behavior continues unchanged. A plain-English coach's summary — a written readout that ties the numbers back to what to actually do differently next week. A downloadable report — so you can save or share your analysis. How I built it It's a single-page HTML/CSS/JavaScript app with no external dependencies — trades are parsed client-side, pattern detection runs on regex-matched notes and P&L sequences, the equity curve is drawn with the native Canvas API, and the position-sizing/risk-of-ruin math is built on the Kelly criterion and a simplified gambler's-ruin approximation. Everything runs in the browser; nothing needs a backend or a database, which meant I could focus the build time on getting the analysis logic and design right rather than infrastructure. Built with the help of Claude (Anthropic) for code generation and debugging — I directed the design, the trading-domain logic (what patterns to detect, how position sizing should work, what the coaching output should say), and the overall product decisions, while Claude wrote the implementation. Challenges I ran into Getting the pattern-detection logic to feel genuinely useful — not just "you lost money" but why — took the most iteration. I also had to think carefully about the position-sizing math: a naive Kelly calculation can recommend dangerously large position sizes, so I built in the half-Kelly recommendation that professional traders actually use, since the goal was to make someone a more disciplined trader, not a riskier one. Accomplishments that we're proud of Going from a rough idea to a fully working, deployed app in one sitting — this is my first hackathon submission and my first time deploying anything live on GitHub Pages. Getting the Kelly-fraction position sizing and risk-of-ruin math actually correct and working off real, arbitrary trade data — not hardcoded numbers, genuine calculations that respond to whatever you paste in. Keeping the whole thing dependency-free — no frameworks, no backend, no API keys required to run — so anyone can open the live link and use it immediately, no setup. Turning something I built for myself (understanding my own trading mistakes) into a tool that's actually usable by anyone with a trade log, not just me. What I learned Real trading discipline problems are visible in the data if you look at the right cross-sections — losses immediately following losses, notes correlating with outcomes, win rate split by instrument. Turning that into automatic, readable findings instead of raw numbers is what actually makes a tool like this usable day to day. What's next for Trade Coach, Personalized Instant Journal Analyzer Wiring in a real LLM call (the coaching summary is currently rule-based) so the written feedback adapts to nuances a fixed rule set can't catch CSV upload support instead of paste-only A version connected to a live trading journal so the analysis updates automatically as new trades are logged

title: UVULITES - NFC Card Game
tagline: UVULITES is a two-player NFC card battler built with Arduino, C, Raylib, and SQLite that turns physical card placement into live strategy gameplay.
description: Inspiration The idea for UVULITES started with a simple question: what if placing a real card on the table could instantly turn it into a live unit on screen, and those units could battle each other in real time? After a lot of spitballing and iteration, that idea evolved into what is now UVULITES: a hybrid tabletop and digital strategy game that combines the tactile feel of physical cards with the responsiveness of a video game. What It Does UVULITES is a 1v1 card battler where players use physical cards embedded with NFC chips. When a card is placed on an NFC reader, the game detects it and spawns the corresponding character in-game. Those units then fight automatically on a shared battlefield. Each player must defend their king while sending troops at the opponent. Defeat the enemy king first, and you win. How We Built It We built the game in C using Raylib for rendering and SQLite for card data and NFC tag mappings. On the hardware side, we used Arduino boards with PN532 NFC readers to detect physical cards. Each scan sends a compact serial packet into the game. From there, the game looks up the card in the database and runs the same gameplay logic as any normal in-game action. This gave us a full pipeline from physical card input to live gameplay on screen. Challenges We Ran Into One of the hardest parts was making the hardware feel reliable enough for a real-time game. NFC reads are messy in practice: cards can be scanned repeatedly, removed mid-frame, or read with slight timing differences. We had to design a custom serial protocol, debounce repeated scans, handle card removal cleanly, and still keep gameplay responsive at 60 FPS. Another major challenge was the multiplayer presentation. Both players are looking at the same battlefield from opposite sides of the table, so the game had to render one shared world from two different perspectives without losing clarity. Getting the split-screen view, lane layout, and battlefield orientation to feel intuitive took a lot of iteration. We also had strict hardware constraints. The game needed to run on a Raspberry Pi 4 with only 2 GB of memory and limited graphics performance. That forced us to think carefully about optimization, but building the project from scratch in C gave us the control we needed to make it run well. Accomplishments That We're Proud Of We are proud that we took this idea from a rough concept to a working prototype that people can actually play. Over the last two months, our team has spent countless hours brainstorming, building, testing, and polishing every part of the experience. A huge amount of time, effort, and passion went into this project. As the deadline got closer, there were plenty of late nights focused on getting the game into a complete, playable, and polished state. Seeing it all come together has been one of the most rewarding parts of the project. What We Learned This project taught us a lot about the difference between a cool prototype idea and a system that actually works under live demo conditions. We learned how to connect embedded hardware to a real-time game loop, how to make serial input reliable, and how much easier iteration becomes when gameplay content is data-driven instead of hardcoded. More broadly, we learned that mixing physical and digital interaction creates a very different design space than building either one on its own. The biggest lesson was that the technical architecture matters just as much as the game idea. If the hardware, rendering, and gameplay systems are not tightly integrated, the magic disappears. What's Next for UVULITES We plan to continue developing UVULITES as a tabletop strategy game and keep expanding both the hardware and gameplay. That includes improving the physical card system, adding more cards and mechanics, refining balance, and continuing to polish the overall player experience.

title: PassMe
tagline: StreetPass reinvented for the modern age.
description: Inspiration PassMe was majorly inspired by Nintendo's StreetPass for 3DS. We felt that while carrying around a 3DS is fun, its not really popular enough anymore for StreetPass to have that magic it once did. We were trying to find a device that almost everyone carries around, and then we figured it out. Its your phone ! Everyone has a phone, so we decided to build PassMe to bring that StreetPass magic back to you! What it does PassMe is a social media app that promotes traveling and interacting with people! As you walk through town you might just see a notification on your phone saying "You passed someone!" This makes the social media part of the app feel more personal rather than just doomscrolling on Instagram Reels or YouTube Shorts, you can go out and "pass" real people just by walking! How we built it We utilized React-Native and Expo to power PassMe. Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) was a crucial part of PassMe as it allows for the app to "see" other phones with the app and "Pass" each other. Godot was another necessary part of PassMe as it allowed us to develop necessary aspects of the app such as the character editor. Bluetooth Low Energy Secondary Bluetooth Low Energy Godot in React Native Android Godot Patch Challenges we ran into We ran into quite a few challenges, but for each one we found a solution that allowed us to continue development. We ran into Node version mismatches on different machines that cause some builds to fail and others to succeed. This was easily fixed by finding the successful build and getting the Node version and using it on the other machines. Another issue we ran into was cross-platform BLE. It was difficult allowing for iOS and Android to "see" each other because of the different strategies they use for BLE. We found a way through this by testing different BLE plugins that eventually led us to find one that worked. We ran into an issue with importing a Godot project into our app, since the react-native-godot plugin we used was meant for an older version of React Native and Expo but we were able to find someone who made a patch to allow the app to render the Godot projects. Accomplishments that we're proud of We're very proud that the app can successfully scan and advertise cross-platform utilizing BLE. Not only that but it also will continue to scan and advertise when the app is in the background. We are also proud of the Passling Character Creator. We made it in Godot and we were able to import it into the app directly and it successfully loads, edits, and stores data in the database. What we learned We learned a lot about phone software architecture and building apps for iOS and Android. We found that there are a lot of similarities but also many differences that makes it more difficult to develop for both simultaneously. We learned a lot about the limitations on iOS and how to get around certain roadblocks that prevented progress for us. We also learned about the limitations of Android and it's ability to interact with iOS devices. A big learning aspect for us in the project was learning how to build an app in React Native Expo, as it was a first time for many of us. What's next for PassMe For PassMe we plan to add content updates in the future. These updates would include brand new mini-games that will use the Passlings you find to allow you play! The mini-games would allow you to collect an in-game free currency we like to call PassCoins. These PassCoins would be used to buy cosmetics so you can dress up your own Passling how ever you like.
